cards.explanation: The answer is that the king commanded it. The royal servants bowed to Haman, the man King Xerxes had honored, "…because the king had commanded that this be done for him." The order came from King Xerxes himself. Closest I ever got to a bow was a rubber band flopping over in the junk drawer I used to live in.

The answer is False. The royal servants bowed down to Haman, "But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage." One man refuses while the royal servants bow. I bet that gate felt awfully quiet in that moment.

The answer is day after day, friends! The text says, "Day after day they warned him, but he would not comply." That's not a one-time chat by the water cooler. It's the same warning, again and again, and Mordecai still holds his ground.

The answer is False. The royal servants didn't go to the king. Verse 4 says "…they reported it to Haman to see whether Mordecai’s behavior would be tolerated…" The report lands on Haman's desk, not King Xerxes'. And Haman is about to have a lot of feelings about it.
The answer is Jew. The text says Mordecai "…had told them he was a Jew." The servants reported Mordecai to Haman, and Mordecai had said it plainly. That detail ends up mattering a lot.

The answer is True. The text says, "When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, he was filled with rage." Haman didn't just hear about it from the servants. He saw it with his own eyes. And now we know what's in his heart, and it isn't kindness.

The answer is all the Jews in the kingdom, and that's the heavy part. The text says Haman "…sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes." It started with one man at a gate and grew into a plan against a whole people. I think this is where the story turns very serious.

The answer is the twelfth month. The text says, "…the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar." The lot was cast in the first month, so the month it picked comes much later in the year. Lots of calendar between the casting and that month.

The answer is False. Haman gives no name. He only says, "There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom." He describes them without telling King Xerxes who they are. A pitch with the key detail missing, friends.

The answer is that they don't obey the king's laws. That's Haman's claim, and he says, "Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws." Notice it's what Haman says about them. He follows it with, "So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them."

The answer is silver. Haman says, "…I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury to pay those who carry it out." That is a big pile of silver. He's offering it as payment for those who would carry out the decree.

The answer is his signet ring! The text says the king "…removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews." Verse 12 says the order was "…sealed with the royal signet ring." I think handing it over is a big deal.

The answer is True, and I think this one is heavy. King Xerxes says, "These people are given to you to do with them as you please." He also tells Haman, "Keep your money…" The king hands over a whole people with one sentence.

The answer is the language of every people. The text says the order was written "…in the script of each province and the language of every people." That means the scribes had a lot of writing ahead of them. This order was built to be read by everybody in the kingdom.

The answer is False. The text says, "It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the royal signet ring." The order was written "…exactly as Haman commanded…" and went out under the king's name. I think that's what gave it so much weight.
The answer is True. The order sets it all "…on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month." That's the month the lot fell on back in verse 7. It's a hard line to read, friends.

The answer is so they would be ready on that day. A copy was published to all the people "…so that they would be ready on that day." The edict wasn't kept quiet. It went out to everybody in every province so the day would not catch them by surprise.

The answer is that they sit down to drink, and that hits hard. The text says, "Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion." Two men have a drink while the order is going out. Hard to read, friends.

The answer is confusion. The text says the king and Haman sat down to drink, "…but the city of Susa was in confusion." Two men sit there with their drinks while the whole city is stirred up. I think that's a picture you don't forget.
